source_refs.note: Book p. 184: 6.3.2 elements 1-6 (axis, vertex, chord/focal chord, focal distance, latus rectum, parametric equations) with Figure 6.12.

items: Axis: The straight line through the focus and perpendicular to the directrix is called axis of the parabola. In the figure, the axis is \(x\)-axis.
Vertex: The point where the axis meets the parabola is called the vertex. In the figure, \(V\) is the vertex with coordinates \((0, 0)\).
Chord and Focal Chord: A line segment joining two distinct points on a parabola is called a chord. A chord passing through the focus is called a focal chord.
Focal Distance: The distance of a point on the parabola from the focus is called its focal distance. In the figure, \(|FP|\) is the focal distance.

Latus Rectum: The focal chord perpendicular to the axis of the parabola is called the latus rectum. Its equation is \(x = a\). It intersects the parabola \(y^{2} = 4ax\) at points where \(y^{2} = 4a^{2}\) that is, \(y = \pm 2a\). Thus, the end points \(L\) and \(L'\) of the latus rectum are \(L(a, 2a)\) and \(L'(a, -2a)\).

blocks.alt: On a pale yellow panel, the parabola y^2 = 4ax (cyan) with magenta X- and Y-axes; the cyan directrix x = -a (arrows at both ends) with the word 'Directrix' written along it; vertex V(0, 0) and focus F(a, 0) (Focus) marked with arrows from their labels; the latus rectum LL' from L(a, 2a) to L'(a, -2a); P(at^2, 2at) (t-point) joined to F; a focal chord through F; and a chord, each labelled along its length.
blocks.caption: Figure 6.12: Elements of the parabola (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 6.12)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Two useful facts that follow (our additions, used in the exercise):
Length of the latus rectum: \(|LL'| = 2a - (-2a) = 4a\). So the number in front of \(x\) in \(y^{2} = 4ax\) is exactly the length of the latus rectum.
Focal distance of \(P(x, y)\): by the definition \(|FP| = |PM| = x + a\) (for \(y^{2} = 4ax\), \(x \ge 0\)). For example, the end \(L(a, 2a)\) of the latus rectum has focal distance \(a + a = 2a\).

items:
Parametric Equations: The equation \(y^{2} = 4ax\) can be expressed parametrically. Let \(\frac{y}{2a} = t\) and \(\frac{2x}{y} = t\). Then \(y = 2at\) and \(2x = yt = (2at)t = 2at^{2}\), So, \(x = at^{2}\). Hence, the parametric equations are
\[x = at^{2},\ y = 2at\]
The point \((at^{2}, 2at)\) lies on the parabola for all real \(t\) and is often referred to as the \(t\)-point.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Check that the \(t\)-point is really on the curve: put \(x = at^{2}\), \(y = 2at\) in \(y^{2} = 4ax\):
\[(2at)^{2} = 4a^{2}t^{2}\]
\[4a(at^{2}) = 4a^{2}t^{2}\]
Both sides agree for every \(t\). Each real \(t\) gives one point: \(t = 0\) gives the vertex, \(t = 1\) gives \(L(a, 2a)\), \(t = -1\) gives \(L'(a, -2a)\). Positive \(t\) gives the upper half, negative \(t\) the lower half. Why use it? One letter \(t\) describes a point, instead of two coordinates tied by an equation; this makes tangent and normal formulas short (Exercise 6.3, Q8).

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: Learn the four numbers of \(y^{2} = 4ax\) together: vertex \((0, 0)\), focus \((a, 0)\), directrix \(x = -a\), latus rectum \(x = a\) of length \(4a\). To find \(a\) from a given equation, compare: \(y^{2} = 12x\) gives \(4a = 12\), so \(a = 3\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Axis: line through the focus perpendicular to the directrix (here \(y = 0\)).
2. Vertex: where the axis meets the curve (here \((0, 0)\)).
3. Chord: joins two points of the curve; focal chord: a chord through the focus.
4. Focal distance of \(P\): \(|FP|\); for \(y^{2} = 4ax\) it equals \(x + a\).
5. Latus rectum: focal chord perpendicular to the axis; \(x = a\), ends \((a, \pm 2a)\), length \(4a\).
6. Parametric form: \(x = at^{2}\), \(y = 2at\); \((at^{2}, 2at)\) is the \(t\)-point.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Taking the length of the latus rectum as \(2a\) (that is only half of it, from \(L\) to \(F\)).
2. Writing the \(t\)-point as \((2at, at^{2})\): for \(y^{2} = 4ax\) the squared parameter goes with \(x\).
3. Calling any chord through the vertex a focal chord. A focal chord must pass through the focus.
